prototype_questions.question: Which active-leader fence and Redis epoch-install protocol prevents a stale gate process from mutating state or issuing accepted permits across PostgreSQL lease loss and delayed Redis writes?
prototype_questions.rationale: The accepted service has separate PostgreSQL latch and Redis state stores. The local probe tested row-lock serialization and Redis stale-epoch rejection separately, but not delayed writes, lease loss, split brain, or permit issuance through one service protocol. Compare candidates with deterministic failure injection before selecting the implementation contract.
decision_criteria: stale leader cannot mutate Redis after a higher epoch is installed
no permit issuance when owner, lease, lock, or epoch is uncertain
bounded recovery when a delayed old-epoch command lands before installation
durable monotonic epoch behavior across REF-Q process restart; provider failover remains a separate PROD-Q qualification
bounded lock duration and simple operational recovery
lost PostgreSQL finalization and uncertain WAITAOF responses remain inhibited until reference-target evidence establishes the exact durable result
coordinated PostgreSQL and Redis restore cannot admit from mutually consistent stale snapshots on a supported wrapper path
each supported REF-Q restore path writes and fsyncs the host inhibit record before restoring either store; direct/provider restore, full-host rollback, and wrapper bypass are outside REF-Q guarantees
the current restore-episode ID invalidates pre-restore commands and permits on supported paths; unavailable or unverified control denies admission
resume release is idempotently bound to the audited RESUME command; admission remains denied until durable release acknowledgement

candidates.approach: Use a PostgreSQL owner/epoch row lock with server-time lease validation across each bounded Redis mutation or permit issue, install the leader epoch in Redis with a monotonic Lua compare-and-set, bind both stores to the externally verified restore-episode ID, and wait for the configured fsync threshold before serving.

Use a PostgreSQL transaction-scoped advisory lock plus a durable owner/epoch row compare-and-set, with the same monotonic Redis epoch installation and fsync barrier; deny work whenever either PostgreSQL signal is uncertain.

prototype_questions.question: How can command retries remain idempotent after one-year actor-audit deletion without retaining actor identity or operator reason indefinitely?
prototype_questions.rationale: PAUSE and RESUME command IDs must not produce duplicate transitions or become reusable with different requests. Actor/reason audit follows accepted retention policy A (minimum 365 days, then deletion within the qualified bounded window); command deduplication has a separate retention design. Prototype the smallest privacy-preserving option and measure storage/restore behavior.
decision_criteria: same command never advances generation twice
changed-request reuse is rejected after audit expiry

actor identity and operator reason are deleted on the accepted A deletion deadline of event time plus at most 365 days + 1 hour + 2 seconds, if epsilon <= 1 second and W <= 1 hour are qualified for every copy
minimal retained data and explainable backup/export deletion
recovery remains fail-closed after Redis or PostgreSQL restore
every authenticated duplicate retry is actor-attributed durably before returning the stored result
retrying the same command with a different audit-only reason returns the original state result, advances no generation, and records that retry separately
long-lived tombstones do not retain recoverable low-entropy operator reasons or require unsafe key retention
MAC rotation remains consistent across PostgreSQL, Redis, and every retained backup at every crash cut
NEW_ONLY cannot be declared while PostgreSQL/Redis tombstone key sets differ or any live tombstone lacks a valid new-key primary MAC
every actor/reason audit copy is securely deleted by its accepted A deadline (365 days plus at most 1 hour + 2 seconds under qualified bounds) without retaining it to preserve tombstones
the qualified timestamp error bound, tamper-evident inherited backup deadline, and restore/promotion rollback checks cannot shorten retention

candidates.approach: Keep a minimal PostgreSQL command tombstone indefinitely, separately from the one-year actor/reason audit, keyed by (restore_episode_id, command_id) and atomically mirrored by the Redis transition-result tombstone. Retain every non-sensitive canonical MAC input (API version, restore episode ID, action, expected latch epoch, expected current Redis generation, barrier generation, and opaque registration ID), keyed request MAC/key ID, and result status/code/generations. Exclude actor, reason, free-text, and personal identifiers. Use resumable cross-store re-MAC rotation with old/new MAC slots; prohibit key retirement until authoritative rows and retained backups have been migrated or expired.

Use a gate-minted immutable, signed request envelope whose opaque command ID binds the canonical request and expiry; deliver the envelope before execution and reject expired envelopes before any store lookup, then delete command-result rows after the maximum retry horizon while preserving one-year actor/reason audit.

prototype_questions.question: Which permit and identity-validation contract lets application instances reject forged, cross-instance, stale, and replayed permits while safely stopping new handlers within the accepted five-second limit during gate-service loss?
prototype_questions.rationale: The accepted design separates workload PAUSE from individual-operator RESUME and uses short-lived generation-bound permits. Issuer/audience validation, instance identity binding, signing-key rotation, and local handler-start validation must be testable without allowing a public ecommerce identity or caller-chosen instance ID to control the global gate.
decision_criteria: workload identity can PAUSE but cannot RESUME
only individually authenticated operators with the dedicated role can RESUME
permit binds verified subject to deployment, instance incarnation, leader, latch, and gate generations
permit binds an unpredictable signed request nonce to its outstanding issuance request
registration and drain proof bind a unique authenticated instance to a broker-observed connection, not caller-supplied identifiers
forged, stale, cross-instance, expired, and replayed permit responses reject; a currently installed valid lease may authorize multiple handler starts until expiry
lost gate connectivity stops new handler starts by the conservative five-second expiry
renewable lease issuance, lease replacement, and PAUSE have a tested linearization point; PAUSE blocks renewal and revoke stops new starts
per-instance lease renewal meets a predeclared replica-count and renewal-rate envelope with bounded latency and overload behavior
late lease responses cannot install a permit after PAUSE; nonce registration, network request, and local install/start increment have tested lock boundaries
permit temporal claims and fresh restore-episode binding are explicit; broker connection record IDs are provider-qualified as non-reusable or admission fails closed

candidates.approach: Use a gate-issued signed renewable short-lived lease with an epoch-scoped signing key and authenticated workload identity binding. A currently installed valid lease may authorize multiple handler starts until its conservative expiry, at most five seconds after the renewal request began. Enforce strict issuer/audience/algorithm/expiry checks and current leader-epoch bootstrap before admission.

Use an opaque permit reference bound to an authenticated instance registration and require an online gate-service admission check at each handler start; this stops earlier than the renewable-lease candidate during gate-service loss and must be evaluated against the accepted five-second availability behavior.

prototype_questions.question: How does the restore wrapper’s durable host inhibit reach every gate permit issuer and application instance, remaining fail-closed across gate restart, lost notification, and partial restore?
prototype_questions.rationale: The accepted REF-Q design puts the restore episode in a root-owned host control record outside the service backup domains, while the gate service issues admission permits. The wrapper must confirm that every issuer observes the current episode before any restore starts, and stale/unavailable observations must deny admission. The observation/acknowledgement path is not selected and can change the reference design.
decision_criteria: wrapper durably records INHIBITED before any supported restore and cannot report success until every active permit issuer confirms the exact episode and generation, or all issuer processes are proven stopped with automatic restart fenced for the restore window
gate restart, lost or delayed notification, partial restore, and stale host-record read never permit admission

permit issuance/install/start is serialized against observation of INHIBITED; an issuer stops new permit responses and acknowledges the exact episode only after pending responses are fenced or reconciled

before any restore, the wrapper obtains a complete barrier-generation inventory of registered app instance incarnations and broker connection identities after registration is frozen, durably binds that inventory to the new episode in the independent host-control record, and denies restore if completeness is uncertain
application drain, readiness-down, and channel closure account for already-issued permits, prefetched deliveries, and active handlers before any service-store restore begins
a stale but well-formed ACTIVE host record is rejected against an independently trusted fresh expected episode/generation; the freshness source and its trust boundary are explicit

all registered app instances stop new handler starts and readiness remains down until audited RESUME for the exact episode; after restoring gate Redis, every registration and drain acknowledgement recovered from that snapshot is stale and cannot satisfy RESUME; re-establish current-episode drain acknowledgements or require an authenticated gate-resume operator to record durable fencing proof through the audited operator tool, bound to the exact deployment, instance, broker connection, and episode; broker-observed closure alone is insufficient

no root write capability is granted to the gate service; exact host path ownership/mode, gate UID/GID/capabilities, path-substitution defense, and record integrity are verified for every candidate; if the candidate mounts the host record, also verify mount identity and read-only enforcement

for process-quiescence candidate C, the exact REF-Q Compose target explicitly sets restart: no for app and gate issuer containers and excludes host-level auto-start during the restore window; wrapper crash or Docker/service restart must not restart stale processes
crash cuts around host-record fsync/rename, gate observation, drain, store restore, audited RESUME, and host-inhibit release reconcile idempotently

if the selected mechanism reads the host record on the admission path, synchronous read latency, failures, and resource cost are measured separately on the accepted reference capacity sweep; process-quiescence alternatives measure shutdown, restart-fence, and recovery costs
host loss, root compromise, full-host rollback, and wrapper bypass remain explicitly outside REF-Q guarantees

candidates.approach: Candidate only; the local mount probe favors a read-only directory mount over an individual-file mount on the observed Docker Desktop host. The wrapper writes a complete temporary record, fsyncs it, atomically renames it over the current record, and fsyncs the directory. Before selection, define and test an independently fresh expected episode/generation, serialize each gate's permit issue/install path against PAUSE observation, fence pending responses before exact-episode acknowledgement, prove deployment least privilege/path integrity, and measure synchronous record-read cost. Unavailable, malformed, stale, or unreadable state denies admission.

Use an authenticated wrapper-to-gate inhibit/release API with durable episode and acknowledgement state; gate restart bootstraps from the host record before it may issue permits, and the wrapper waits for every issuer acknowledgement. A gate that has not observed the current episode must deny permits; an API-only notification path is insufficient after a lost request unless an additional fresh host-control signal prevents stale ACTIVE admission.

Candidate only; after durably recording the new INHIBITED episode, the wrapper freezes new registrations at the gate barrier, obtains the complete barrier-generation inventory of app instance incarnations and broker connection identities, and durably stores that inventory with the episode in the independent host-control record. It denies restore if the inventory cannot be proven complete. The wrapper then blocks external admission, drains app instances and closes Rabbit consumer channels, and stops every app and gate issuer process. Before restoring any store it verifies all inventoried instances and issuers are stopped, broker connections are closed, and the local supervisor/restart policy cannot start stale processes during the restore window. It restarts the gate through a protected wrapper-controlled path bound to the exact host-record episode in sticky INHIBITED mode and reconciles restored stores. After a gate-Redis restore, it treats every restored registration and drain ACK as stale and requires new durable fencing proof through the audited operator tool for the union of the host-record barrier inventory and any registration recovered from Redis, bound to the exact deployment, instance, broker connection, and episode. This covers instances omitted by an older snapshot. This candidate does not allow the fresh-app-ACK alternative on that path: apps are stopped and the gate protocol does not define registration during PAUSE. Broker-observed closure alone is insufficient and stopping a container is not proof. Only after proofs and durable audited RESUME does it release the host inhibit and start apps. Missing/stale startup binding or any uncertain inventory denies restore or admission. This avoids per-permit mount polling but shifts the proof burden to process-manager fencing, startup binding, and crash recovery; wrapper bypass, root compromise, and full-host rollback remain excluded.

prototype_questions.question: Can a deployment-owned RabbitMQ fencer block a synthetic workload principal from reconnecting, bind its incarnation to broker-generated connection and consumer identities, prove settled drain, and prevent an old handler's protected synthetic effect during a concurrent fence while remaining inhibited on uncertainty?
prototype_questions.rationale: The current decision evidence establishes that RabbitMQ's built-in close permission is broader than the required operation-scoped capability and that client connection names are untrusted. Harness review identified additional required evidence: block the principal before close, use broker-generated connection/consumer identities rather than channel numbers or client tags, prove drain from agreeing broker sources or events, and race a transactional conditional effect against the fence. This is a disposable research prototype only; it does not implement the application consumer or authorize admission.
decision_criteria: The operation-scoped fencer blocks the registered Rabbit principal before close, refuses a reconnect using it, closes every existing connection under it, and leaves unrelated principals untouched; its authority covers both block and close.

The registration binds authenticated workload incarnation and principal/vhost to broker node, broker-generated connection name and broker-generated consumer tag. Channel numbers and client-chosen tags are diagnostic only; ambiguity refuses fencing.

Drain is acknowledged only when /api/connections, /api/channels and /api/consumers agree continuously for a target-recorded settle interval, or a selected broker event source proves the equivalent terminal state.
A handler already executing when the broker connection closes remains a live process; its stale ACK is rejected and its unacked synthetic delivery is redelivered.

The protected effect uses a conditional write in the same database transaction as the generation check, serialized with the fence generation transition. Concurrent tests cover both effect-first and fence-first orderings; no stale effect commits after fence completion.
Fencer timeout, lost response, stale observation, or uncertain close result leaves admission inhibited and cannot be converted to a drain acknowledgement.
The fencer identity cannot read or export quarantine payloads; any broad management authority is recorded as a limitation and prevents a least-privilege pass claim.
The application AMQP consumer remains disabled; all broker messages and protected effects are synthetic and isolated from application data.
Evidence records exact RabbitMQ image digest, broker/client versions, commands, raw observations, and limitations; no result qualifies REF-Q or PROD-Q.

candidates.approach: A fixed-operation isolated fencer service mediates RabbitMQ, holds the broker credential, blocks new authentication/use for the registered principal, resolves an authenticated workload registration to the broker node, broker-generated connection name and broker-generated consumer tag, closes every existing connection under that principal, and confirms settled drain. Its capability covers both principal block and exact close. The prototype must expose residual administrator authority and cannot claim least privilege unless the service boundary and negative tests prove the accepted deployment capability.

A broker-side authorization extension exposes block-principal, inspect-exact and close-principal-connections operations with operation-scoped authorization and an independently authenticated workload-to-connection/consumer registration. The prototype may model this only if the extension is not available locally; a model is not broker evidence and leaves the candidate unqualified.

prototype_questions.question: Can a disposable RabbitMQ broker-side plugin fence one registered consumer incarnation with narrow authority and serialize principal revocation against in-progress authentication and session registration?
prototype_questions.rationale: Harness closed P-005's integration-boundary review and accepted this candidate for a bounded experiment. P-005's completed reconnect run remains immutable diagnostic evidence only. This experiment isolates the unresolved broker capability: a unique principal per incarnation, a scoped operation, an authoritative PostgreSQL fence generation, and a deterministic authentication race. It is a scratch prototype only; no application fencer, consumer, gate, or framework is implemented or enabled.
decision_criteria: Use the pinned RabbitMQ 4.1.8 image and synthetic identities/data only; compare a per-incarnation principal revoked by native user deletion against the disposable plugin candidate, without treating the administrator baseline as an acceptable fencer identity.

The named deployment provisioner and its credential are separate from the mTLS fencer identity; record the provisioner's actual privileges and keep any broader bootstrap authority outside the fencer. The fencer resolves only an immutable registered incarnation-to-principal mapping and cannot create users, change mappings, enumerate users, read message bodies, or alter topology/permissions.

The plugin accepts only fence(incarnation_id, expected_generation, request_id) and produces FENCED, GENERATION_MISMATCH, UNKNOWN_INCARNATION, PARTIAL, or FAILED; transport timeout/error is UNKNOWN to the caller.

FENCED is accepted only with exact matching incarnation_id, expected_generation, request_id, a revocation record, and zero sessions after reconciliation; every other result, mismatched echo, or nonzero count yields no drain acknowledgement and leaves the synthetic admission coordinator INHIBITED.

A request_id is bound to the complete request tuple; exact replay with the same tuple returns the original revocation record, while reuse with a different incarnation_id or expected_generation is rejected. Lower generations never report success; PARTIAL or FAILED never roll revocation back.

With rabbitmq_auth_backend_cache disabled or explicitly invalidated, a TCP proxy deterministically pauses the old principal's handshake after connection.start-ok, before connection.open, and before the first channel opens while fencing runs; after exact FENCED no old session may survive or reconnect, and the new principal remains usable.

PostgreSQL fence_generation is the only authority for protected synthetic business effects. The sequence is close admission, advance the database generation, fence the broker principal, verify drain, then audited resume; a conditional synthetic effect is rejected if fencing won serialization and any effect that won first commits before the generation advance.

For the single-node experiment only, reconcile the broker's session state after revocation and record the observation method; this is diagnostic evidence, not an accepted production drain interval or cluster-wide proof.

All spike source and runtime artifacts remain disposable and isolated; no application AMQP consumer, production fencer, gate change, shared framework extension, migration, or REF-Q/PROD-Q/S30-06 qualification claim results from this prototype.

candidates.approach: Baseline: one RabbitMQ principal per consumer incarnation, revoked through native user deletion by a separately held test provisioner/admin credential. This demonstrates the behavior available from RabbitMQ's documented built-in revocation and is not a least-privilege fencer design.

Disposable, version-pinned broker-side plugin exposes only the incarnation-scoped fence operation, serializes revocation against authentication/session registration, and returns the typed idempotent result. Compare it with A using the same synthetic handshake schedule and negative-authorization tests.

prototype_questions.question: Can the existing Candidate C host restore wrapper block a stale-episode restart and provide distinct process-exit, CAS-refusal, broker redelivery/drain, and credential-reuse evidence on the current Docker Desktop target without a new controller or service?
prototype_questions.rationale: One bounded synthetic feasibility attempt was requested after the RabbitMQ plugin was deselected. The experiment must first identify an existing executable wrapper and stale-episode start guard. If either is absent, or an authorized Docker user can bypass the wrapper, stop before starting a container and report the blocker; do not build control infrastructure.
decision_criteria: Before runtime, identify the exact existing wrapper command, controlled launch paths, controller identity/permissions, and stale-episode refusal. restart: no is not a start authorization guard; explicitly document the Docker-user bypass boundary.
If there is no existing wrapper/start-block mechanism, or proof requires a new privileged service, mark the run BLOCKED before runtime and recommend deferring S30-06.
If preflight permits the run, use only one isolated disposable Compose project, pinned synthetic images/data, unique run labels/names, bounded commands, and cleanup limited to this run.
Report process termination and stale-episode restart refusal separately; capture container state/PID, restart policy/count, daemon events, and the controller's refusal for the old episode.

In a separate CAS scenario, hold a synthetic handler before its protected write, advance the database generation, then allow the write attempt and record the CAS refusal. This result must not depend on killing the handler.

In a separate broker scenario, kill the consumer container with a synthetic delivery unacknowledged; inspect connections, channels, consumers, unacknowledged count, and redelivery after a bounded settle interval. Container exit alone is not drain evidence.

Before the run, define credential-test interpretation: if the old Rabbit credential authenticates outside the stopped container, access revocation is UNSATISFIED. Do not weaken that criterion or assume secret isolation after observing the result.
Record each result independently; no aggregate PASS, production claim, consumer enablement, accepted-spec change, Harness change, purchase, or remote Git operation is in scope.

candidates.approach: Candidate C process isolation using only the already-existing versioned host restore wrapper and its current start-control mechanism. No new controller, service, daemon, VM, or privilege proxy is allowed.
